claim: Tg(gata3:loxP-DsRed-loxP:GFP) and Tg(gata3:Gal4) transgenic lines were generated from bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC) insertion transgenesis.
source: To provide transgenic labeling of the V2b population, we generated two gata3 transgenic lines, Tg(gata3:loxP-DsRed-loxP:GFP) and Tg(gata3:Gal4) from bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC) insertion transgenesis.
evidence: The manuscript describes the generation method for these transgenic lines.

claim: Both gata3 transgenic lines label V2b neurons throughout the rostrocaudal extent of the larval zebrafish spinal cord.
source: Both lines label V2b neurons throughout the rostrocaudal extent of the larval zebrafish spinal cord (Figure 1A; Tg(gata3:loxP-DsRed-loxP:GFP) line shown).
evidence: The manuscript states this directly and references Figure 1A showing the labeling pattern.

claim: Gata3-driven fluorescent proteins are broadly expressed in the brain, hindbrain, and assorted non-nervous system soft tissue including the pronephric duct.
source: Gata3-driven fluorescent proteins are also broadly expressed in the brain, hindbrain, and assorted non-nervous system soft tissue including the pronephric duct (Wingert et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript describes the expression pattern and cites a reference for the pronephric duct expression.

claim: Each hemisegment contains on average 17.2 ± 2.5 V2b neuron somata.
source: On average, each hemisegment contained 17.2 + /- 2.5 (mean + /- SD) V2b neuron somata with relatively little variation from rostral to caudal segments (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data with mean and standard deviation, and references Figure 1C.

claim: All 59 V2b neurons traced had axons that descended caudally and ipsilaterally.
source: In all 59 neurons, the axon descended caudally and ipsilaterally, with an extent ranging from 2 to 15 segments.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative anatomical data from traced neurons.

claim: V2b axons extend from 2 to 15 segments in length.
source: In all 59 neurons, the axon descended caudally and ipsilaterally, with an extent ranging from 2 to 15 segments.
evidence: The manuscript provides the range of axon lengths observed.

claim: No V2b neurons extended rostral axons beyond the segment of origin.
source: However, in contrast to V2a neurons (Menelaou et al., 2014; Azim et al., 2014), no V2b neurons extended rostral axons beyond the segment of origin.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation and contrasts it with V2a neurons.

claim: Axonal projections are longest for V2b somata located in the midbody range relative to V2b located in the rostralmost and caudalmost segments.
source: Single-cell Kaede photoconversions made at different positions along the rostrocaudal extent of the spinal cord revealed that axonal projections were longest for V2b somata located in the midbody range relative to V2b located in the rostralmost and caudalmost segments (Figure 1E and F, p=3.17×10−3 and p=4.44×10−4, ANOVA and Tukey's test).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of axon length data with p-values and references figures.

claim: V2b neurons in embryonic zebrafish are exclusively inhibitory and predominantly GABAergic.
source: Previous work has established that V2b neurons in embryonic zebrafish, as identified by Gata3 RNA expression, are exclusively inhibitory and predominantly GABAergic (Batista et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work establishing this finding.

claim: Nearly all larval V2b neurons expressed Glyt2 in 5 dpf larvae.
source: Nearly all larval V2b neurons expressed Glyt2 in 5 dpf larvae (Figure 2A), in contrast to embryonic stages.
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation and references Figure 2A.

claim: Gad1b is expressed in approximately half of the V2b population in 5 dpf larvae.
source: In contrast, Gad1b is expressed in approximately half of the V2b population (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation and references Figure 2B.

claim: Gad1b and Glyt2 expression in V2b neurons remains unchanged from 5 to 15 dpf, with ~52% of neurons expressing Gad1b and ~91% expressing Glyt2.
source: Gad1b and Glyt2 expression in V2b neurons remains unchanged across these ages, with ~52% of neurons expressing Gad1b and ~91% expressing Glyt2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data on neurotransmitter expression stability and references Figure 2C.

claim: There are at least two subclasses of V2b neurons: those expressing Glyt2 but not Gad1b, and those expressing both Glyt2 and Gad1b.
source: These ratios indicate at least two subclasses of V2b neurons: those expressing Glyt2 but not Gad1b, and those expressing both Glyt2 and Gad1b.
evidence: The manuscript infers subclasses from the neurotransmitter expression data.

claim: GABAergic V2b somata are located slightly ventral to non-GABAergic V2b somata on average.
source: By plotting dorsal-ventral (DV) position relative to spinal boundaries, we found that on average, GABAergic V2b somata are located slightly ventral to non-GABAergic V2b somata, but that both populations span the same DV range (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative positional data and references Figure 2D.

claim: The percentage of GABAergic V2b cells is highest (~80%) in rostral segments, then decreases to ~50% by midbody and throughout the rest of the spinal cord.
source: In the rostrocaudal axis, the percentage of GABAergic V2b cells is highest (~80%) in rostral segments, then decreases to ~50% by midbody and throughout the rest of the spinal cord.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data on the rostrocaudal distribution of GABAergic V2b cells.

claim: Glyt2 robustly colabels with V2b cells throughout the entire spinal cord.
source: In contrast, Glyt2 robustly colabels with V2b cells throughout the entire spinal cord (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation and references Figure 2E.

claim: GABAergic V2b-mixed neurons project axons ventrally along the spinal cord, with an average axon location between 0.24–0.33 DV.
source: GABAergic V2b-mixed neurons projected axons ventrally along the spinal cord, with an average axon location found between 0.24–0.33 DV (example, Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative anatomical data and references Figure 3A.

claim: Axons from V2b-gly neurons typically make an initial ventral dip but then turn more dorsally, ranging from 0.31 to 0.65 in the DV axis.
source: In contrast, axons from V2b-gly neurons typically make an initial ventral dip but then turn more dorsally, ranging from 0.31 to 0.65 in the DV axis (example, Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative anatomical data and references Figure 3B.

claim: The axon DV position of V2b-gly neurons is positively correlated to the soma DV position.
source: The axon DV position of V2b-gly neurons is positively correlated to the soma DV position, that is a more dorsal soma projects a more dorsally positioned axon (Figure 3G).
evidence: The manuscript reports a correlation analysis and references Figure 3G.

claim: V2b-mixed cells project axons ventrally to a narrow spinal cord region regardless of soma position.
source: However, this trend is not realized for V2b-mixed cells, which project axons ventrally to a narrow spinal cord region regardless of soma position.
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation contrasting V2b-mixed with V2b-gly neurons.

claim: Motor neurons active during fast movements are located more dorsally within the spinal cord, whereas those for slower movements are located more ventrally.
source: Previous work has shown that motor neurons active during fast movements are located more dorsally within the spinal cord, whereas those for slower movements are located more ventrally (McLean et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work establishing this organizational principle.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation in the Tg(gata3:Gal4; UAS:CatCh) line is sufficient to elicit action potentials in V2b neurons.
source: We first validated that optogenetic stimulation in the Tg(gata3:Gal4; UAS:CatCh) line was sufficient to elicit action potentials in V2b neurons (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports validation experiments and references Figure 4A.

claim: Optogenetic activation of V2b neurons elicits robust IPSCs in motor neurons.
source: Optogenetic activation of V2b neurons with a 20–50 ms pulse of light delivered 3–7 segments rostral to the recording site elicited robust IPSCs in motor neurons (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological recordings and references figures.

claim: Synaptic conductance amplitudes from V2b to motor neurons exhibited a median of 139 pS (25–75% range, 97–174 pS).
source: Synaptic conductance amplitudes exhibited a median of 139 pS (25–75% range, 97–174 pS).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative electrophysiological data.

claim: Localized light stimuli targeting V2b but not CSF-cN or ISN somata elicited reliable IPSCs in both primary and secondary motor neurons.
source: To validate that V2b neurons are providing these inhibitory inputs, we used a digital micromirror device to deliver targeted squares of light stimuli (~20 μm x 20 μm) to dorsal spinal cord areas containing V2b but not CSF-cN or ISN somata. These localized stimuli still elicited reliable IPSCs in both primary and secondary motor neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports control experiments and references supplementary figures.

claim: In animals with strong CatCh expression in CSF-cNs and negligible expression in V2b neurons, full-field light stimulation did not evoke IPSCs in motor neurons.
source: As a second control, recordings were also made in a subset of animals with strong CatCh expression in CSF-cNs and negligible expression in V2b neurons (see Materials and methods and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D). In these recordings, even full-field light stimulation did not evoke IPSCs in motor neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports control experiments and references supplementary figures.

claim: The optogenetically elicited inhibitory inputs to motor neurons arise from monosynaptic V2b to motor neuron connections.
source: Together these results indicate that the optogenetically elicited inhibitory inputs arise from monosynaptic V2b to motor neuron connections.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this based on the control experiments described.

claim: Strychnine blocked a median of 91% of the V2b-evoked IPSC in fast motor neurons.
source: Bath application of 10 µM strychnine to block glycine receptors abolished a median of 91% of the V2b-evoked IPSC in fast motor neurons, but only 71% of the V2b-evoked IPSC in slow motor neurons (Figure 4D and E,C; p=0.003, Wilcoxon Rank test).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative pharmacological data with statistical analysis and references figures.

claim: Strychnine blocked only 71% of the V2b-evoked IPSC in slow motor neurons.
source: Bath application of 10 µM strychnine to block glycine receptors abolished a median of 91% of the V2b-evoked IPSC in fast motor neurons, but only 71% of the V2b-evoked IPSC in slow motor neurons (Figure 4D and E,C; p=0.003, Wilcoxon Rank test).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative pharmacological data with statistical analysis and references figures.

claim: The GABAA receptor antagonist gabazine eliminated the remaining IPSC after strychnine application in all cases.
source: The GABAA receptor antagonist gabazine (SR-95531, 10 µM) eliminated the remaining IPSC in all cases.
evidence: The manuscript reports pharmacological results.

claim: V2b-mediated inhibition onto fast motor neurons is carried out predominantly by glycinergic synapses.
source: Therefore V2b-mediated inhibition onto fast motor neurons is carried out predominantly by glycinergic synapses, whereas V2b inhibition onto slow motor neurons is carried by mixed glycinergic/GABAergic transmission.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: V2b inhibition onto slow motor neurons is carried by mixed glycinergic/GABAergic transmission.
source: Therefore V2b-mediated inhibition onto fast motor neurons is carried out predominantly by glycinergic synapses, whereas V2b inhibition onto slow motor neurons is carried by mixed glycinergic/GABAergic transmission.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: V2b activation did not change thresholds or gain relationships on average in both fast and slow motor neurons.
source: Interestingly, V2b activation did not change thresholds or gain relationships on average, in both fast and slow motor neurons (Figure 4F).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological results and references Figure 4F.

claim: Optogenetic activation of rostrally-located V2b neurons evoked IPSCs in 11/21 (52%) mid-body V2b neurons.
source: Optogenetic activation of rostrally-located V2b neurons evoked IPSCs in 11/21 (52%) mid-body V2b neurons (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative connectivity data and references figures.

claim: The median conductance of individual IPSCs from V2b to V2b was 158 pS (25–75% range, 84–203 pS).
source: The median conductance of individual IPSCs was 158 pS (25–75% range, 84–203 pS).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative electrophysiological data.

claim: Application of strychnine blocked a median of 80% of the V2b-evoked IPSC in V2b neurons, while the remainder was abolished by gabazine.
source: Application of strychnine blocked a median of 80% of the V2b-evoked IPSC, while the remainder was abolished by gabazine (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: The manuscript reports pharmacological results and references figures.

claim: Some V2b neurons inhibit other members of the V2b pool, forming a disinhibitory pathway.
source: Thus, some V2b neurons inhibit other members of the V2b pool, forming a disinhibitory pathway.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from the connectivity data.

claim: V2b neurons were silent at rest.
source: V2b neurons were silent at rest, in contrast to CSF-cNs which exhibited spontaneous spiking (data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological observations.

claim: There was no difference in input resistance between V2b-gly and V2b-mixed neurons.
source: There was no difference in input resistance (Figure 5F) or spike shape (Figure 5G) between the V2b-gly and V2b-mixed neurons.
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological comparisons and references figures.

claim: There was no difference in spike shape between V2b-gly and V2b-mixed neurons.
source: There was no difference in input resistance (Figure 5F) or spike shape (Figure 5G) between the V2b-gly and V2b-mixed neurons.
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological comparisons and references figures.

claim: The two V2b subpopulations are indistinguishable at the level of intrinsic physiology despite their anatomical differences.
source: Therefore, the two V2b subpopulations are indistinguishable at the level of intrinsic physiology despite their anatomical differences.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from the electrophysiological comparisons.

claim: A CRISPR-generated Tg(gata3:ZipACR-YFP) knock-in shows robust expression of the fluorescent ZipACR protein in V2b neurons and ISN but only sparse, dim expression in CSF-cNs.
source: However, a CRISPR-generated Tg(gata3:ZipACR-YFP) knock-in shows robust expression of the fluorescent ZipACR protein in V2b neurons and ISN but only sparse, dim expression in CSF-cNs (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of transgene expression and references Figure 6A.

claim: CSF-cN expression of ZipACR-YFP was observed exclusively in the apical extension into the central canal but not the soma.
source: CSF-cNs expression was observed exclusively in the apical extension into the central canal but not the soma (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations and references figures.

claim: Under low-intensity light conditions, action potentials were completely suppressed in 4 out of 6 V2b cells and partially suppressed in one additional cell.
source: Under lower-intensity light conditions, identical to those of the behavioral recordings, action potentials were completely suppressed in 4 out of 6 V2b cells and partially suppressed in one additional cell (Figure 6B and C), in Tg(gata3:ZipACR-YFP; gata3:loxP-DsRed-loxP:GFP) animals.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative electrophysiological validation data and references figures.

claim: Identical low-intensity light stimulation partially suppressed spiking in only 1 of 5 CSF-cNs.
source: In contrast, identical stimulation partially suppressed spiking in only 1 of 5 CSF-cNs (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative electrophysiological validation data and references figures.

claim: The total tail displacement and quantity of tail movements did not significantly differ during optogenetic stimulation of V2b neurons.
source: The total tail displacement and quantity of tail movements did not significantly differ during optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6D and F).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral analysis results and references figures.

claim: Tail beat frequency increased in Tg(gata3:ZipACR-YFP)+ animals during light stimulation but not in their ZipACR negative clutchmates.
source: Strikingly, tail beat frequency (TBF), a proxy for locomotor speed (Müller and van Leeuwen, 2004), increased in Tg(gata3:ZipACR-YFP)+ animals during light stimulation but not in their ZipACR negative clutchmates (Figure 6E and G, paired Student's t-test p=0.0025).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative behavioral data with statistical analysis and references figures.

claim: The average TBF change during V2b suppression was 1.4 Hz (control TBF mean = 13.4 Hz, stimulation TBF mean = 14.7 Hz).
source: The average TBF change was 1.4 Hz (control TBF mean = 13.4 Hz, stimulation TBF mean = 14.7 Hz) and was robustly observed in animals from three clutches.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative behavioral data.

claim: Suppression of V2b neurons increases locomotor frequency.
source: We conclude that suppression of V2b neurons increases locomotor frequency.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from the behavioral experiments.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation rostral to the ventral root recordings, targeting V2b neurons, led to a decrease in the first inter-burst interval relative to trials without light stimulation.
source: Optogenetic stimulation rostral to the ventral root recordings, targeting V2b neurons that provide inhibition to the recorded segment, led to a decrease in the first inter-burst interval (IBI) relative to trials without light stimulation (Figure 7D and E, paired Student's t-test p=1.72×10−4).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative electrophysiological data with statistical analysis and references figures.

claim: IBIs across the entire swim bout were reduced in frequency during V2b activation.
source: IBIs across the entire swim bout, which progresses from faster to slower, were also reduced in frequency (Figure 7F, p=1.51×10−3, paired Student's t-test) though to a lesser degree than the first IBI (Mann-Whitney Wilcoxon test p=1.23×10−3).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data with statistical analysis and references figures.

claim: Caudal optogenetic stimulation did not affect IBI frequency.
source: First, to test whether connections from CSF-cNs could slow locomotion, optogenetic activation was delivered caudally to the recorded segment, to target the predominantly ascending axons of CSF-cNs. Caudal stimulation did not affect IBI frequency (Figure 7G and H, paired Student's t-test, p=0.495).
evidence: The manuscript reports control experiment results with statistical analysis and references figures.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation in low V2b CatCh expressing animals did not lead to a significant change in tail frequency.
source: Optogenetic stimulation in low V2b CatCh expressing animals did not lead to a significant change in tail frequency (Figure 7E, paired Student's t-test p=0.174, CatCh- sibling control group p=0.427).
evidence: The manuscript reports control experiment results with statistical analysis and references figures.

claim: Red-shifted light stimulation did not vary tail beat frequencies from controls.
source: Finally, to determine whether visually-induced effects contributed to the locomotor slowing, we delivered a red-shifted excitation (~550 nm) incapable of activating CatCh to rostral segments in the normally-expressing Tg(gata3:Gal4; UAS:CatCh) line. Tail beat frequencies of the red-shifted stimulation did not vary from controls (Figure 7G and H, paired Student's t-test, p=0.467).
evidence: The manuscript reports control experiment results with statistical analysis and references figures.

claim: Activation of V2b neurons reduced swim bout duration.
source: Activation of V2b neurons in the original experiment did reduce swim bout duration (Figure 7I, Student's t-test p=4.65×10−3).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data with statistical analysis and references figures.

claim: Stimulating V2b neurons reduces the speed of rhythmic tail movements during swim.
source: All together these experiments demonstrate that stimulating V2b neurons reduces the speed of rhythmic tail movements during swim.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from the experimental results.

claim: V2b neurons play a role in speed control in motor circuits by acting as a brake on locomotor frequency.
source: In combination with our finding that V2b suppression increased swim frequency, these results provide evidence that V2b neurons play a role in speed control in motor circuits by acting as a brake on locomotor frequency.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from the combined optogenetic manipulation experiments.

claim: The V2b population comprises two stable subclasses, defined by neurotransmitter identity: one subclass is exclusively glycinergic and the other mixed glycinergic/GABAergic.
source: In this study we demonstrate that V2b neurons exert direct control over axial musculature in the larval zebrafish. The V2b population comprises two stable subclasses, defined by neurotransmitter identity: one subclass is exclusively glycinergic and the other mixed glycinergic/GABAergic.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes this finding in the Discussion.

claim: V2b subclasses synapse directly onto motor neurons with differential targeting to speed-specific circuits.
source: These V2b subclasses synapse directly onto motor neurons with differential targeting to speed-specific circuits.
evidence: The manuscript states this in the Abstract as a summary of findings.

claim: Suppressing V2b neurons elicits faster locomotion.
source: In vivo, optogenetic manipulation of V2b activity modulates locomotor frequency: suppressing V2b neurons elicits faster locomotion, whereas activating V2b neurons slows locomotion.
evidence: The manuscript states this in the Abstract as a summary of findings.

claim: Activating V2b neurons slows locomotion.
source: In vivo, optogenetic manipulation of V2b activity modulates locomotor frequency: suppressing V2b neurons elicits faster locomotion, whereas activating V2b neurons slows locomotion.
evidence: The manuscript states this in the Abstract as a summary of findings.

claim: V2b neurons serve as a brake on axial motor circuits.
source: We conclude that V2b neurons serve as a brake on axial motor circuits.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion in the Abstract.

claim: Ipsilateral inhibition plays a role in speed control.
source: Together, these results indicate a role for ipsilateral inhibition in speed control.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion in the Abstract.

claim: Zebrafish V2b neurons are inhibitory.
source: We demonstrated that V2b neurons are inhibitory and extend axons ipsilaterally and caudally in zebrafish (Figures 1 and 3) similar to V2b neurons in mice (Lundfald et al., 2007; Britz et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding in the Discussion and cites supporting figures and references.

claim: Zebrafish V2b neurons extend axons ipsilaterally and caudally.
source: We demonstrated that V2b neurons are inhibitory and extend axons ipsilaterally and caudally in zebrafish (Figures 1 and 3) similar to V2b neurons in mice (Lundfald et al., 2007; Britz et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding in the Discussion and cites supporting figures and references.

claim: Mouse V2b neurons extend axons ipsilaterally and caudally.
source: We demonstrated that V2b neurons are inhibitory and extend axons ipsilaterally and caudally in zebrafish (Figures 1 and 3) similar to V2b neurons in mice (Lundfald et al., 2007; Britz et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites references for mouse V2b neuron anatomy.

claim: Gata3+ V2b neurons are widely present in vertebrates.
source: Gata3+ V2b neurons are widely present in vertebrates but have also been identified in the nerve cord of a marine annelid, indicating an ancestral persistence in motor circuitry (Karunaratne et al., 2002; Vergara et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites references for the presence of V2b neurons across species.

claim: Gata3+ neurons have been identified in the nerve cord of a marine annelid.
source: Gata3+ V2b neurons are widely present in vertebrates but have also been identified in the nerve cord of a marine annelid, indicating an ancestral persistence in motor circuitry (Karunaratne et al., 2002; Vergara et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites references for the presence of Gata3+ neurons in annelids.

claim: Gata3-expressing cells in the embryonic 24 hr post fertilization zebrafish are predominantly GABAergic with a smaller subset expressing or co-expressing glycine.
source: Gata3-expressing cells in the embryonic 24 hr post fertilization zebrafish are predominantly GABAergic with a smaller subset expressing or co-expressing glycine (Batista et al., 2008), an inversion of our finding that V2b cells in 5–15 dpf zebrafish are all glycinergic with approximately half co-expressing GABA.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference for embryonic zebrafish V2b neurotransmitter expression.

claim: Early in development, murine V2b neurons broadly co-express GABA and glycine.
source: Early in development, murine V2b neurons broadly co-express GABA and glycine (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference for mouse V2b neurotransmitter expression.

claim: By P0 in mouse, nearly all V2bs are glycinergic and ~25% are GABAergic.
source: By P0 in mouse, however, nearly all V2bs are glycinergic and ~25% are GABAergic (Lundfald et al., 2007), which is broadly similar to our results.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference for postnatal mouse V2b neurotransmitter expression.

claim: The differential expression of the transcription factors Gata2/Gata3/BhlhB5 in non-overlapping neural subsets in mouse may imply the presence of V2b subpopulations.
source: However, the differential expression of the transcription factors Gata2/Gata3/BhlhB5 in non-overlapping neural subsets may imply their presence (Francius et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference and speculates about V2b subpopulations in mouse.

claim: Genetically and anatomically distinct subclasses have been identified within the V0, V1, and V2a populations in mouse and zebrafish.
source: More broadly, our finding of subclasses in the V2b population is parallel to previously identified genetically and anatomically distinct subclasses within the V0, V1, and V2a populations in the mouse and zebrafish (Bikoff et al., 2016; Hayashi et al., 2018; Menelaou et al., 2014; Song et al., 2018; Björnfors and El Manira, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites references for subclasses in other spinal interneuron populations.

claim: V2b (Gata3+) neurons are thought to correlate to ventral longitudinal (VeLD) neurons.
source: V2b (Gata3+) neurons are thought to correlate to ventral longitudinal (VeLD) neurons, an anatomically defined cell class with a characteristic longitudinal ventral-positioned axon (Batista et al., 2008; Hale et al., 2001; Bernhardt et al., 1992).
evidence: The manuscript cites references for the relationship between V2b and VeLD neurons.

claim: In mice, the V2 progenitor domain gives rise to a third class of neurons called V2c, which express Sox1 and only transiently Gata3 in very early development (prior to E12.5) before later downregulation.
source: In mice, the V2 progenitor domain gives rise to a third class of neurons called V2c, which express Sox1 and only transiently Gata3 in very early development (prior to E12.5) before later downregulation (Panayi et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference for V2c neurons in mouse.

claim: Sox1a/b is present in the 24 hpf zebrafish spinal cord and colabels with Gata3.
source: It is unclear whether zebrafish have a homologous V2c population, although Sox1a/b is present in the 24 hpf spinal cord and notably also colabels with Gata3 (Andrzejczuk et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference for Sox1a/b expression in zebrafish.

claim: A possible V2c homolog, referred to as V2s, has been identified as a Sox1a/b+ glycinergic cell type deriving from the V2 domain with long, ipsilateral, caudally projecting axons.
source: A possible V2c homolog, referred to as V2s, has been identified as a Sox1a/b+ glycinergic cell type deriving from the V2 domain with long, ipsilateral, caudally projecting axons (Gerber et al., 2019) similar to the V2b-gly neurons described here.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference for V2s neurons in zebrafish.

claim: Locomotion at faster versus slower speeds engages different sets of spinal interneurons, both within a genetically defined population and across populations.
source: Locomotion at faster versus slower speeds engages different sets of spinal interneurons, both within a genetically defined population (McLean and Fetcho, 2009; McLean et al., 2008; Ampatzis et al., 2014; Zhong et al., 2011) and across populations (McLean et al., 2007; Talpalar et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites references for speed-dependent recruitment of spinal interneurons.

claim: Glycine receptor-mediated currents traditionally show faster decay rates than those from GABA receptors in much of the nervous system.
source: In much of the nervous system, glycine receptor-mediated currents traditionally show faster decay rates than those from GABA receptors (Awatramani et al., 2005), including at interneuron inputs onto motor neurons (Jonas et al., 1998; O'Brien and Berger, 1999; Russier et al., 2002); with some exceptions (Dumoulin et al., 2001; Eggers and Lukasiewicz, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites references for glycine and GABA receptor kinetics.

claim: GABA can act as a coagonist on glycine receptors and shorten the postsynaptic inhibitory response.
source: Moreover, GABA can act as a coagonist on glycine receptors and in fact shorten the postsynpatic inhibitory response (Lu et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference for GABA's action on glycine receptors.

claim: Fast and slow motor neurons have overlapping dendritic fields despite their different somatic positions.
source: One caveat in interpretation of these results is that despite their different somatic positions, fast and slow motor neurons have overlapping dendritic fields (Svara et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference for motor neuron dendritic anatomy.

claim: One role of ipsilateral inhibition is to mediate flexor-extensor alternations via Ia reciprocal inhibition from V2b and V1 populations.
source: One role of ipsilateral inhibition is to mediate flexor-extensor alternations via Ia reciprocal inhibition from V2b and V1 populations (Britz et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites references for the role of V2b and V1 in flexor-extensor alternation.

claim: Genetic ablation of V1 neurons in mouse and larval zebrafish both led to a reduction in fictive locomotor speeds.
source: In contrast, genetic ablation of V1 neurons in mouse and larval zebrafish both led to a reduction in fictive locomotor speeds (Gosgnach et al., 2006; Kimura and Higashijima, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites references for the effects of V1 ablation.

claim: In-phase V1 inhibition limits slow motor neuron recruitment during fast movements through both direct and indirect (V1 onto V2a) synaptic pathways.
source: In-phase V1 inhibition was found to limit slow motor neuron recruitment during fast movements through both direct and indirect (V1 onto V2a) synaptic pathways (Kimura and Higashijima, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference for V1 inhibition mechanisms.

claim: Inhibition in-phase with excitation increases for increasingly strong movements.
source: Measuring inhibitory conductances in motor neurons in vivo has revealed, surprisingly, that inhibition in-phase with excitation actually increases for increasingly strong movements (Kishore et al., 2014; Berg et al., 2007; Berg et al., 2008; Li and Moult, 2012), rather than diminishing to allow more powerful contractions.
evidence: The manuscript cites references for in-phase inhibition during movement.

claim: Ipsilateral inhibition may act to isolate movements in certain behaviors that engage dedicated premotor circuitry, for example through the selective inhibition of interneurons during scratching versus swimming in turtle.
source: Thirdly, ipsilateral inhibition may act to isolate movements in certain behaviors that engage dedicated premotor circuitry, for example through the selective inhibition of interneurons during scratching versus swimming in turtle (Berkowitz, 2002; Berkowitz, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites references for behavior-specific inhibition in turtle.

claim: Gata3 is expressed in cerebrospinal fluid contacting neurons (CSF-cN).

claim: V2b neurons in larval zebrafish are exclusively inhibitory.
source: To describe the neurotransmitter profile of V2b neurons in larvae, Gata3+ neurons were evaluated for coexpression with transgenic markers for glyt2, a glycine vesicular transport protein, and gad1b, a GABA synthesis enzyme. Nearly all larval V2b neurons expressed Glyt2 in 5 dpf larvae (Figure 2A), in contrast to embryonic stages. In contrast, Gad1b is expressed in approximately half of the V2b population (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript shows all V2b neurons express inhibitory neurotransmitter markers (Glyt2 and/or Gad1b), implying they are exclusively inhibitory.
